newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close mostly higher in light trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close mostly higher in light trade.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended a lackluster session mostly higher Tuesday as market participants awaited the results of a policy makers' meeting in Washington.
The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) was widely expected to leave monetary policy unchanged when it announced its decision at about 1415 EST/1915 GMT Wednesday.
Yet few investors chose to stake positions prior to the announcement, as a tightening was not completely ruled out and before the release of January payrolls data Friday.
The 30-year long bond ended 13/32 higher at 97-11/32. Its yield fell to 6.71 percent from 6.74 percent late Monday.

"There was nothing going on. It was really, really quiet out there, the kind of day when you have to double down on the amount of caffeine you're taking just to stay awake," said Steven Wood, economist at BancAmerica Securities Inc.

Wood added that he didn't think a lot of short positions were being established ahead of expectations the Fed would leave policy unchanged, meaning there was little potential for a significant "relief trade" should the FOMC not act.
The bond market was unlikely to break out of Tuesday's doldrums soon, Wood said. Though there could be some position setting Thursday, no breakout was seen until Friday, he said.
"The estimates for this number are all over the place. Typically two-thirds to three-quarters of those surveyed are within 25,000 of the consensus, but this month it's less than half," Wood said.

A Reuters consensus called for the creation of 237,000 payrolls, a 5.2-percent jobless rate, and a 0.2-percent gain in average hourly earnings. Howevr, Wood noted his calls ranged anywhere from less than 100,000 to more than 400,000.

"Today the market obviously focused on FOMC and as long as there was even a little uncertainty the market wasn't going to move much in either direction," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Bank.

The March bond contract pushed above resistance at 112 midafternoon, and the long end of the curve received some support from that and the unwinding of some corporate hedges, traders said. The three-month sector underperformed the rest of the curve, however.
Sohn looked for a payrolls increase of 350,000 due to the five-week survey period in January.
"More and more it seems to becoming a trend that the market doesn't react to minor economic data releases," Sohn said.

Wednesday the Treasury will announce the size of its quarterly refunding. Analysts polled by Reuters expected, on average, the refunding effort to total $37.5 billion made up of $17.5 billion of three-year notes, $10 billion of 10-year notes and $10 billion of 30-year bonds.
Helping to support bond prices were signals of progress toward agreement on a balanced U.S. budget by 2002. President Clinton's State of the Union was scheduled for Tuesday night.
Jerry Zukowski, economist at PaineWebber Inc., said the strength seen late in the session came amid very thin trading conditions and weren't indicative of a trend higher.
"We just sort of had a very gentle drift up, but it didn't mean much as volume was so low," Zukowski said.

Also on Tuesday, the two-year note was unchanged at 100-even and yielded 5.87 percent; the five-year closed up 2/32 at 100-9/32 and yielded 6.18 percent, and the 10-year note closed up 4/32 at 100-16/32 to yield 6.43 percent.
